16 OCTOBER 2026 · DESIGN REVIEW AFTER SINGLE-PHOTO LAYOUT PASS

Clearer navigation.
Still too much interface.

Yes, there is still avoidable space. Yes, filters should become directly visible. The next pass should replace the existing control stacks with a coherent, contextual tool system.

The single-photo mobile model is a useful improvement. The remaining gap to the references is consistency: information hierarchy, compact tool options, discoverable creative choices and predictable transitions. This is a review and action plan, not an implemented redesign or a usability-study result.

iPhone: reclaim useful space

The supplied screenshot still feels divided into large blocks. Exposure occupies one control area, Filters & Fix another, then the toolbox another. The large Fit capsule also competes with the photograph. The filename is truncated despite the generous header appearance.

  • Top area: the blank band is visible in the supplied image and hosted captures. Verify its real-device safe-area/navigation contribution before removing anything. Preserve status-bar and camera clearance. Avoid stacking a second title or custom toolbar beneath native navigation.
  • Filename: omit the “Demo ·” prefix from the scarce title space; disclose demo status in the document menu. Keep the full filename in document details and accessibility.
  • Adjust: replace the separate Filters & Fix row with a compact parameter selector, slider, numeric value and reset. Keep a Details control in that same surface.
  • Toolbox: make Adjust, Filters, Crop, Retouch and More directly reachable with labels. Validate five targets at the narrowest supported width and provide a readable accessibility variant.
  • Fit: use a smaller secondary zoom control or reveal it with canvas interaction; keep a persistent accessible route. Do not let it obscure the photo unnecessarily.
  • History: provide obvious Undo while editing; avoid making every correction require a visit to More. Compare can support press-and-hold as an additional shortcut, with a discoverable button retained.

Proposed standard-text target: one approximately 44-point navigation row below the system safe area, a roughly 64–80-point Adjust surface and a 56–64-point toolbox above the home inset. These are starting budgets, not fixed accessibility heights. Relative to the current 110-point Adjust container, reducing that container alone to 72 points would return 38 points to the canvas.

Filters should be a destination, not a submenu

Current route: Adjust → Filters & Fix → Photo Filters → another presentation. The name combines creative exploration with automatic correction, and no filter previews are visible in the editing workspace.

Recommendation: Filters is a first-class toolbox item. Opening it replaces Adjust controls with a horizontal strip of Original plus our six existing looks, named thumbnails of the current photo, selected state and a strength control. Keep previews visible while selecting, then dismiss or collapse when returning to another tool. Do not permanently show filters while cropping, drawing or retouching. Keep Auto Enhance/Quick Fix as a separate correction action.

Photomator explicitly documents an automatically opened presets bar with Color Adjustments on Mac, iPad and iPhone, plus a way to hide it. Borrow its direct visual discovery; retain Ameluma’s simpler independent look/strength model and scoped Undo. Do not add more filters before making the six existing ones easy to use.

Photomator’s preset-bar documentation

iPad: one rule for every tool

Landscape: use the side rail plus an adjacent compact options surface. Portrait: use the bottom toolbox plus controls directly above it. Apply that rule to Adjust, Filters, Crop, Retouch, annotations, masks and watermarking. Existing tools mix floating cards, popovers and drawing presentations; their visual transitions still feel like different products.

For retouching, keep Heal/Clone, brush size and Set Source near the selected tool. Put infrequent parameters behind Details. Avoid the wide instructional banner across the photo; guidance belongs in a short contextual hint that disappears after use or in Help.

Portrait-photo side margins are often a consequence of fitting the full image. Use an available margin for options when possible; do not automatically crop the photo to make a density metric look better. Reposition options when zooming would place the working region beneath them.

Photoshop documents contextual tool options that can be moved and docked. Affinity documents a context toolbar and Studio panels. The common lesson is proximity and predictable context—not that floating panels are inherently good or bad.

Mac: compact, but still uneven

Keep the compact document tabs; tabs are not the main Mac problem. The single Exposure control inside a comparatively wide floating surface underuses the available inspector area. Filters remain hidden. Some controls look like native form widgets while others are custom floating cards.

  • Use a consistent resizable inspector for detailed adjustment groups; offer a compact contextual mode for quick edits. Avoid displaying both with duplicate actions.
  • Give Filters a direct rail entry and visual strip or inspector section. Keep strength and Original local to it.
  • Align labels, values and reset controls to shared columns. Use one heading scale and a predictable disclosure hierarchy.
  • Keep tab, toolbar and inspector densities coordinated; use tooltips and keyboard commands rather than shrinking hit areas indiscriminately.

Browsing and batch work

  • Browsing: consolidate count and selection controls into one compact row; make search expandable or use a native search presentation where appropriate. Keep active filtering visible and preserve hidden selections.
  • Grid: offer a dense browsing presentation with consistent cells and smaller gutters. An optional filled thumbnail preview must be clearly separate from actual crop/output geometry. Preserve full-image framing previews in Frame mode.
  • Batch: retain the affected count and make Change Photos the single clear way to replace captured inputs. Consolidate redundant scope controls and secondary View options.
  • Eight photos on a tall iPad: empty space after the last row is not itself a defect. The opportunity is a larger adjustable thumbnail size and a compact persistent settings entry, not stretching the photos or adding filler.
  • Terminology: distinguish workspace filtering from creative photo filters in labels and navigation. Keep Resize and Convert easy to find without duplicating Editor.

P1Consistent tool-options placementSide rail → adjacent options; bottom dock → options above. Test every tool, portrait/landscape, keyboard, Split View and large text. Draft Apply/Cancel remains explicit.
P2Browse and batch densityFewer header bands; larger first-screen photo area; clear active/selected/batch states; filters never change captured operation inputs.
P2Final visual consistencyCommon spacing, aligned values, restrained surfaces, direct removal/reset actions, readable contrast and meaningful accessible labels.

Capture identical demo sources in portrait and landscape, light and dark, standard and accessibility text. Compare fitted images at the same geometry. Exercise tap → edit → Undo → Back → reopen → export. Inspect actual device status/navigation/home insets before claiming pixel savings. No new processing tools or architecture rewrite is needed.

Evidence and limits

This report reviews the supplied screenshot, source implementation and the native capture sets generated immediately after the single-photo editor pass. No new app rendering or build was performed for this review. Sources: /tmp/ameluma-single-editor-{mac,ipad,phone}-images. The report embeds reduced, uncropped copies for offline use. Mac captures omit native window chrome. Hosted mobile captures use controlled sizes and safe-area behavior; they do not prove real-device status-bar spacing or touch usability.

Competitor images are published product/documentation references previously acquired locally, with official pages rechecked for this review. They are not fresh hands-on captures, matched zoom comparisons, or evidence that every release uses identical UI. Affinity is specifically the Photo 2 reference; no Affinity iPhone counterpart is asserted. Different image aspect ratios prevent fair raw canvas-percentage ranking.
